summary: Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to interconnected physiological and behavioral health risks. AURORA is an interactive astronaut health-monitoring and mission-intelligence platform designed to help crews recognize, investigate, and respond to changes in their health throughout extended space missions. Combining personalized health baselines, explainable anomaly detection, multivariable analysis, mission simulation, and an immersive orbital research station, AURORA transforms individual health measurements into understandable trends and relationships.Its signature feature, SIGNAL VEIL, allows users to visually uncover and investigate connections between health indicators, while the Constellation Engine identifies meaningful patterns that may not be apparent from individual measurements alone.Using reproducible synthetic astronaut data informed by NASA research and scientific literature, AURORA demonstrates how onboard health monitoring could support astronaut self-assessment and informed decision-making when immediate medical support from Earth is limited.
details:
AURORA: Every Signal Counts

AURORA (Autonomous Understanding of Risk, Observation & Astronaut Resilience) is a browser-based astronaut health-monitoring and mission-intelligence platform designed for the challenges of long-duration human spaceflight. It helps astronauts monitor their health, recognize unusual changes, investigate relationships between health indicators, and explore how mission conditions may affect crew well-being.

AURORA combines individual health self-assessment, crew health analytics, explainable anomaly detection, interactive data visualization, and mission simulation into one integrated application.

How it works

AURORA provides astronauts with a self-assessment interface where they can manually enter eight health readings, including blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, and mood. Measurements are displayed against explanatory reference ranges, with guidance on why each reading matters and what follow-up may be appropriate.

The Crew Health Analytics system organizes 15 indicators into five categories: cardiovascular health, sleep, physical health, radiation exposure, and behavioral health. Users can examine historical trends, compare crew members, and review changes throughout a mission.

At the center of the platform is the Constellation Engine, a statistical analysis system that looks beyond isolated measurements. It establishes individual baselines, tracks deviations over time, identifies multiple indicators changing together, and evaluates relationships between signals. Its explainable alerts show which measurements changed, when the changes occurred, and why a pattern was flagged. Users can also record responses and examine before-and-after trends without automatically assuming that an intervention caused the change.

AURORA's signature feature, SIGNAL VEIL, transforms this analysis into an interactive experience. Presented as a fog-covered astronaut visor, it allows users to clear the fog and explore health indicators as a constellation of connected signals. Users can inspect individual measurements, draw connections between signals, scrub through the mission timeline, and replay how patterns developed. The visualization is driven by the same data and analysis used throughout the application.

The platform also includes Mission Control, which summarizes mission progress, crew status, alerts, and significant events; a What-If Simulator that compares baseline and hypothetical mission conditions across seven health indicators; and a local, rule-based Mission Assistant that answers questions by analyzing the loaded mission data.

Finally, AURORA includes an interactive first-person orbital research station with eight connected modules and five functional consoles. Its medical, environmental, navigation, and communications interfaces connect to the same underlying mission data used by the rest of the platform.

Benefits and intended impact

Long-duration missions create situations in which astronauts must understand changes in their own health while operating far from immediate medical support. Individual measurements may not reveal gradual changes or patterns involving several different health indicators.

AURORA aims to make this information easier to understand and investigate. Personal baselines help highlight changes relative to an individual's historical measurements, while multivariable analysis can reveal patterns that isolated thresholds might miss. Explanations accompanying alerts help users understand why something was flagged rather than simply presenting a warning.

Our intended impact is to demonstrate how integrated health-monitoring software could support astronaut self-awareness, earlier recognition of unusual trends, more informed discussions with medical support, and better exploration of health-related mission scenarios.

Creativity and innovation

AURORA's creativity lies in combining statistical health analysis with an immersive, interactive way of exploring data.

SIGNAL VEIL is designed around the idea that important health patterns are not always visible when measurements are examined independently. Instead of presenting another conventional dashboard, it allows users to uncover signals, explore their relationships, and replay how patterns emerge over time.

The interactive flight deck extends this concept into a spacecraft environment, making health monitoring part of the mission experience rather than a disconnected collection of charts. The Constellation Engine provides the analytical foundation behind these visual features, connecting the experience to actual application data rather than decorative demonstrations.

Tools and technologies

AURORA was developed as a browser-based application using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. Its technical components include WebGL2 and GLSL for interactive visual rendering, Canvas 2D as a rendering fallback, Recharts for data visualization, Framer Motion for interface transitions, and Vitest for automated testing.

The flight deck uses procedural WebGL2 rendering rather than a prebuilt 3D game engine. The Constellation Engine and simulation logic are implemented in TypeScript. User state is stored locally in the browser, and the application can run without a required backend, account, or external AI service. An optional panel retrieves public space-weather event information through NASA's DONKI API.

Factors considered

Throughout development, our team prioritized scientific transparency, explainability, usability, and performance.

We considered the importance of individual differences between astronauts, the possibility of noisy or incomplete measurements, the difficulty of identifying gradual changes, and the need to distinguish meaningful statistical patterns from medical diagnoses. We also considered the limitations of publicly available spaceflight datasets and the importance of clearly identifying synthetic information.

All crew measurements, mission events, and demonstration anomalies are synthetic. Their design and approximate magnitudes are informed by published spaceflight research, but they are not actual astronaut medical records. The simulator is an illustrative model, not a clinically validated prediction system. AURORA is intended to demonstrate an exploratory approach to astronaut health monitoring, not to replace professional medical judgment or established flight-medicine procedures.
